metadata.title: Eye Care in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU)

authors.name: Hugh Montgomery
authors.role: Professor; Consultant in Intensive Care Medicine

quality_flags: The red, sticky eye summary calls for escalation if there is no improvement in 24 HOURS, while the conjunctivitis section specifies 48 hours.
metadata.summary: This guidance helps ICU staff protect vulnerable patients’ eyes, recognize ocular disease that may require ophthalmic assessment, and administer prescribed eye treatments. It focuses on ocular surface problems while also addressing less common, sight-threatening conditions and ocular involvement in systemic fungal infection. It includes advice for ophthalmologists assessing patients in ICU.

tap and inject using protocol of amikacin and vancomycin

toxicities.event: Exposure keratopathy and corneal epithelial defects
toxicities.incidence: Exposure keratopathy affects 20-42% of ICU patients. Among patients sedated for >48hours, 60% develop corneal epithelial defects, including 42% within the first week.
recognition: Incomplete eyelid closure or markedly reduced blinking increases the risk of corneal drying.
The eye may be red; fluorescein dye reveals epithelial defects.
Persistent defects may lead to corneal scarring, perforation in severe cases, or secondary microbial keratitis.
toxicities.grading: Eyelid-exposure assessment: Grade 0, eyelids fully closed; Grade 1, conjunctiva exposed without corneal exposure; Grade 2, any corneal exposure.

management.actions: Lubricate the eye and close the eyelids with tape or another suitable method.

management.severity: Redness, discharge, chemosis or corneal abnormality
management.actions: Notify medical staff, consider ophthalmological assessment and increase lubrication to every 2 hours.

prevention: Assess eyelid closure and eye appearance with a bright light at least once per shift.
Apply lubricating ointment into the eye four times daily; drops alone do not last as long.
For a conscious patient, 2 hourly lubricant drops and ointment before sleep are an alternative.
When taping is necessary, ensure the lids close completely and the tape does not contact the ocular surface.

recognition: The eye becomes red, and fluorescein dye shows an epithelial defect, most clearly under blue light.
An abrasion that does not improve in 24hrs requires medical staff notification.

management.actions: Treatment can consist of chloramphenicol ointment four times daily for 5 to 7 days, increased lubrication and eyelid taping if unwanted corneal exposure is significant.

prevention: Before securing closed eyelids, check that eyelashes do not rub against the cornea.
Prevent direct pressure on the eyes when nursing a patient prone.

recognition: The conjunctiva becomes swollen and protrudes.
Swelling may interfere with eyelid closure; incomplete closure can also predispose to chemosis.
In severe oedema, the swollen conjunctiva may protrude between closed eyelids.

management.severity: Severe oedema with conjunctiva protruding between closed eyelids
management.actions: Contact medical staff because temporary eyelid closure with sutures may be needed.

prevention: Monitor eyelid closure and protect the ocular surface in patients at risk.

toxicities.event: Eyelid, facial skin or ocular injury from eye coverings
recognition: Repeated tape removal may irritate or injure facial skin or eyelids.
Tape touching the ocular surface, eyelashes rubbing the cornea, or a dry or poorly positioned dressing may damage the eye.
prevention: Use eyelid tape only when needed, with the eyelids fully closed, eyelashes clear of the cornea and tape away from the ocular surface.
A 10x10cm square of cling film over each eye can replace tape; change it every shift.
If oedema prevents manual eyelid closure, hydrogel or silicone dressings or pads may replace tape, but they require careful positioning, protection from drying and replacement once per shift.

toxicities.event: Ocular ischaemia and permanent visual loss
recognition: Severe or recurrent hypotension may cause blindness from ischaemic optic neuropathy. Profound hypotension sustained for extended periods may cause visual loss from ischaemic optic neuropathy or cortical blindness.

In patients nursed prone, direct ocular pressure or increased intraocular or orbital pressure, particularly with periocular swelling or concurrent systemic hypotension, may impair ocular perfusion and lead to ischaemic optic neuropathy or vascular occlusion.
Orbital apex syndrome may cause visual loss from optic neuropathy together with ophthalmoplegia involving multiple cranial nerves.

management.severity: Ocular pressure in a patient nursed prone
management.actions: Relieve pressure on the eyes where possible.

prevention: Avoid direct ocular compression during prone care; the document describes a 3-pin head holder, gel rings or similar devices.

toxicities.event: Bilateral acute glaucoma during prone nursing
recognition: A sudden increase in intraocular pressure may rapidly cause visual loss.
The cornea becomes cloudy and grey, and the pupil remains mid-dilated and does not respond to light.
prevention: Relieve pressure on the eyes during prone nursing where possible.

recognition: Visual aura may occur during voriconazole treatment.

management.actions: The document states that the aura resolves completely after the drug is stopped but is not, by itself, an indication to stop treatment.

toxicities.dose_modifications: Visual aura alone is not an indication to stop voriconazole.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Inspect eyelid closure and eye appearance with a bright light at least once per shift throughout the ICU stay; alert medical staff about redness, discharge, chemosis or corneal abnormalities, consider ophthalmological review and increase lubrication to every 2 hours.

For Grade 1 exposure, lubricate the eye. Apply lubricating ointment into the eye four times daily rather than onto closed eyelids. For a conscious patient, 2 hourly lubricant drops with ointment before sleep are an alternative.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with Grade 1 exposure or otherwise requiring ocular-surface protection

prophylaxis.recommendation: For Grade 2 exposure, combine lubrication with tape or another means of closing the eyelids. Use tape only when needed; close the lids fully, keep eyelashes off the cornea and prevent tape from touching the eye.

Every 4 hours, wash away dried ointment with warm water, inspect the eye under a bright light, and place fresh ointment between the lowered lower eyelid and the conjunctiva. If taping is needed, apply ointment first, close the lids, check eyelash position, clear ointment from the outer eyelids and secure them horizontally with Micropore tape.

A 10x10cm square of cling film over each eye can replace tape; change it every shift and do not share a roll between patients. If oedema prevents manual closure, hydrogel or silicone dressings or pads may be used carefully instead of tape; replace them once per shift and do not allow them to dry or shift into a harmful position.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients needing eyelid protection, including those whose oedema prevents manual closure

prophylaxis.recommendation: For an unconscious patient nursed prone, reapply ocular lubricant every 4 hours and secure the eyelids with tape or cling film. Check corneal clarity with a bright light and notify medical staff if it is abnormal. Avoid direct ocular compression with a 3-pin head holder, gel rings or similar devices.

prophylaxis.type: Prevention of ocular infection during endotracheal suctioning
prophylaxis.recommendation: Perform endotracheal suctioning from the patient's side rather than above the head, with the eyes covered, to reduce Pseudomonas infection rates.

When several eye drops are prescribed, separate medications by ideally 5 minutes and at least 1 minute so one does not wash out another. Administer drops before ointment because ointment hinders their entry into ocular tissues. If lid closure is poor, manually close the lids after ointment instillation to spread it across the eye.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients prescribed multiple eye drops or ocular ointment

infection_management.prevention: Recognise its potential to spread to other patients and staff. Use separate gauze for each eye when cleaning discharge.
infection_management.management: Consider swabbing ocular discharge for microbial culture. Clean discharge from the eyelids with warm water and apply chloramphenicol ointment into the eye four times a day for 5-7 days. If culture suggests resistance but the eye is improving, do not change treatment; if redness or discharge persists, an ointment containing an antibiotic to which the organism is sensitive may be substituted, or other antibiotic drops may be added alongside simple lubricant ointment. The main text requires medical staff notification and ophthalmic help if redness and discharge have not markedly improved in 48 hours; the later eye-care table instead says to alert medical staff if there is no improvement in 24 HOURS. Seek urgent ophthalmological advice if the cornea becomes dull or develops a white patch.

infection_management.prevention: Protect the corneal surface from exposure and injury. When keratitis is present, try to avoid eyelid taping because it may encourage bacterial growth, while maintaining generous ointment lubrication.
infection_management.management: Obtain urgent ophthalmic help for a red eye with a corneal ulcer or white, grey or yellowish opacity. Ophthalmologists are advised to obtain a corneal scrape and immediately begin appropriate intensive topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic therapy; the document notes that virulent bacteria, particularly pseudomonas, are most likely.

infection_management.prevention: During endotracheal suctioning, approach from the patient's side rather than the head and cover the eyes.
infection_management.management: For keratitis, the document advises an immediate corneal scrape and appropriate intensive topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic therapy.
Seek urgent ophthalmic help if corneal dendrites, fluorescein-staining ulcers or non-staining grey corneal areas are observed.

Seek immediate ophthalmic help if endophthalmitis is suspected, particularly when a hypopyon is visible. Ophthalmologists should be guided by a known systemic infection; otherwise, the document advises urgent ocular sampling and injection under its amikacin and vancomycin protocol. If platelet count is <30,000, request platelets before the procedure because of vitreous haemorrhage risk.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Systemic fungal infection with possible intraocular infection
infection_management.prevention: Routine ophthalmic screening of every patient with a positive fungal culture is not indicated. Decide whether and when to examine an individual patient according to symptoms, ocular appearance, risk, prognosis, microbiology results, ocular penetration of current or planned treatment, patient position and feasibility of examination.
infection_management.management: An awake patient without symptoms does not need an examination; an awake patient with symptoms or one unable to report symptoms may need one. Examine a patient with a very abnormal eye appearance, such as hypopyon, a cloudy pupil or possible ocular perforation. For confirmed intraocular infection, coordinate with microbiologists and ophthalmologists to select an appropriate antifungal with good ocular penetration.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Endophthalmitis associated with aspergillus in cystic fibrosis
infection_management.management: In a patient with cystic fibrosis and endophthalmitis, consider aspergillus first as the cause; the document specifies voriconazole as first-line therapy.

therapies_index.name: ointment lubricants
approved_indications: Protection of eyes at risk of corneal damage from incomplete lid closure or reduced blinking.
therapies_index.administration: Apply generously to the eye surface four times daily; before each application, remove residual ointment and inspect the eye. For an unconscious patient nursed prone, reapply every 4 hours.
monitoring: Inspect the eye with a bright light before reapplication.

therapies_index.name: simple eye ointment
approved_indications: Ocular lubrication when corneal protection is needed.
Lubrication alongside other antibiotic drops when indicated by conjunctivitis culture results.
therapies_index.administration: Place the ointment on the eye surface between the lower lid and conjunctiva; ointment lubricants are used four times daily.

therapies_index.name: Lacrilube
approved_indications: Ocular lubrication to protect an exposed eye.
therapies_index.administration: The guidance lists it among ointment lubricants applied to the eye four times daily.

therapies_index.name: Xailin Night
approved_indications: Ocular lubrication to protect an exposed eye.
therapies_index.administration: The guidance lists it among ointment lubricants applied to the eye four times daily.

therapies_index.name: VitA-POS
approved_indications: Ocular lubrication to protect an exposed eye.
therapies_index.administration: The guidance lists it among ointment lubricants applied to the eye four times daily.

therapies_index.name: lubricant drops
approved_indications: An alternative lubrication approach for a conscious patient, with ointment before sleep.
therapies_index.administration: Instil every 2 hours in a conscious patient and apply ointment before sleep. Drops do not persist as long as ointment.

therapies_index.name: Hylotears
approved_indications: Lubrication for a conscious patient as an alternative to regular daytime ointment.
therapies_index.administration: The guidance gives it as an example of lubricant drops used every 2 hours, with ointment before sleep.

therapies_index.name: manual closure of the eyes
approved_indications: Closure of incompletely shut eyelids.
Spreading ointment across the eye surface after instillation when lid closure is poor.
therapies_index.administration: Close the lids manually after instilling ointment when closure is poor; manual closure alone is less effective than correctly applied ointment.

therapies_index.name: taping the eyes shut
approved_indications: Protection when the cornea is exposed in Grade 2.
Eye protection for an unconscious patient nursed prone.
therapies_index.administration: Instil ointment first, close the lids completely, ensure the lashes do not touch the cornea, remove ointment from the external lid surface, and apply Micropore tape horizontally across the lids. Use only when necessary.
key_toxicities: Repeated tape removal may injure or irritate facial or eyelid skin.
Tape touching the eye, incomplete lid closure or lashes rubbing the cornea can cause ocular injury.
Lid taping may encourage bacterial growth when keratitis is present.
monitoring: Check that the lids remain fully closed and the lashes are clear of the cornea.

therapies_index.name: cling film
approved_indications: An alternative to tape for protecting an eye requiring lid closure.
therapies_index.administration: Place a 10x10cm square over each eye and replace it every shift; do not share a roll between patients.

therapies_index.name: hydrogel or silicone dressings or pads
approved_indications: An alternative to lid taping when oedema prevents manual lid closure.
therapies_index.administration: Replace once per shift and use with particular care.
key_toxicities: A dried-out or poorly positioned dressing or pad can damage the eye.
monitoring: Check that the dressing or pad stays moist and correctly positioned.

therapies_index.name: Kerrapro
approved_indications: An example of a dressing or pad that may replace taping when oedema prevents manual lid closure.
therapies_index.administration: Change once per shift.
key_toxicities: A dried-out or incorrectly positioned dressing or pad can injure the eye.

therapies_index.name: Gelliperm
approved_indications: An example of a dressing or pad that may replace taping when oedema prevents manual lid closure.
therapies_index.administration: Change once per shift.
key_toxicities: A dried-out or incorrectly positioned dressing or pad can injure the eye.

therapies_index.name: bathing the eyes with warm water
approved_indications: Removal of dried ointment before another application.
Removal of eyelid discharge in conjunctivitis.
therapies_index.administration: Before renewing ointment, bathe the eyes with warm water; for conjunctivitis, clean each eye with separate gauze.

therapies_index.name: 3-pin head holder
approved_indications: Avoidance of direct eye compression in an unconscious patient nursed prone.

therapies_index.name: gel rings
approved_indications: Avoidance of direct eye compression during prone positioning.

therapies_index.name: temporarily closed with sutures
approved_indications: Possible eyelid closure when severe oedema causes swollen conjunctiva to protrude through the closed lids.
therapies_index.administration: Medical staff should be contacted to assess whether temporary suturing is needed.

therapies_index.name: chloramphenicol ointment
approved_indications: A simple corneal abrasion without secondary infection.
Bacterial conjunctivitis in the ICU.
therapies_index.administration: Apply in the eye four times daily for 5 to 7 days for a simple abrasion, or four times a day for 5-7 days for conjunctivitis. For conjunctivitis, the ointment formulation maintains lubrication.
monitoring: For conjunctivitis, assess discharge and redness for marked improvement within 48 hours.
If culture suggests resistance but the eye is improving, the guidance advises against changing treatment; persistent stickiness or redness may warrant a change.

therapies_index.name: ointment containing an antibiotic to which the organism is sensitive
approved_indications: Conjunctivitis that remains sticky or red when culture suggests the organism is not sensitive to chloramphenicol.
therapies_index.administration: Use in place of chloramphenicol ointment when indicated by the eye's condition and microbial sensitivity.
monitoring: Use microbial culture results and the eye's clinical response.

therapies_index.name: other antibiotic drops
approved_indications: An alternative for conjunctivitis that remains sticky or red when microbial results suggest lack of sensitivity to chloramphenicol.
therapies_index.administration: May be used alongside simple lubricant ointment.

therapies_index.name: intensive topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic therapy
approved_indications: Keratitis assessed by an ophthalmologist.
therapies_index.administration: Start immediately after obtaining a corneal scrape; the guidance does not give a dose or dosing interval.

therapies_index.name: G tropicamide 1%
approved_indications: Pupil dilation for ophthalmic examination in the ICU.
therapies_index.administration: Administer as dilating eye drops.
key_toxicities: Pupils may remain unresponsive to light for about 4 hours after dilation.
monitoring: Record the administration time and the anticipated period of reduced pupillary light responsiveness.

therapies_index.name: G. phenylephrine 2.5%
approved_indications: Pupil dilation for ophthalmic examination in the ICU.
therapies_index.administration: Administer as dilating eye drops.
key_toxicities: Pupils may remain unresponsive to light for about 4 hours after dilation.
monitoring: Record the administration time and the anticipated period of reduced pupillary light responsiveness.

therapies_index.name: amikacin
approved_indications: Use in the tap-and-inject protocol for suspected endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis when systemic infection does not guide treatment.
therapies_index.administration: The guidance specifies use with vancomycin in an urgent tap-and-inject procedure but gives no dose.

therapies_index.name: vancomycin
approved_indications: Use in the tap-and-inject protocol for suspected endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis when systemic infection does not guide treatment.
therapies_index.administration: The guidance specifies use with amikacin in an urgent tap-and-inject procedure but gives no dose.

therapies_index.name: tap and inject using protocol of amikacin and vancomycin
approved_indications: Urgent management of suspected endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis when systemic infection does not guide treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Perform urgently; if the platelet count is <30,000, request platelets before the procedure because of the risk of vitreous haemorrhage.
key_toxicities: Vitreous haemorrhage is a procedural risk when the platelet count is <30,000.
monitoring: Check the platelet count before the procedure.

therapies_index.name: platelets
approved_indications: Administration before a tap-and-inject procedure if the platelet count is <30,000.
therapies_index.administration: Request platelets before the procedure when the platelet count is <30,000.

therapies_index.name: voriconazole
therapies_index.mechanism: The guidance identifies voriconazole as a cytochrome P450 inhibitor and relates this property to visual aura.
approved_indications: First-line therapy for suspected aspergillus endophthalmitis in a patient with cystic fibrosis.
key_toxicities: Visual aura that resolves completely after the drug is stopped; the guidance states that aura alone is not an indication to stop it.

therapies_index.name: appropriate antifungal which has good ocular penetration
approved_indications: Intraocular infection associated with systemic fungal infection.
therapies_index.administration: Select treatment in consultation with microbiologists and ophthalmologists.

therapies_index.name: extra intraocular treatment
approved_indications: The guidance mentions it as a possible treatment requirement in intraocular fungal disease, while stating that disease requiring such treatment is very uncommon.

therapies_index.name: vitrectomy
approved_indications: The guidance mentions it as a possible treatment requirement in intraocular fungal disease, while stating that disease requiring it is very uncommon.

therapies_index.name: endotracheal suctioning
approved_indications: When suctioning is performed, modifying the technique may reduce ocular Pseudomonas infection rates.
therapies_index.administration: Perform suctioning from the patient's side rather than above the head, with the eyes covered.
key_toxicities: Aerosols from suctioning and direct catheter contact are implicated as possible sources of ocular surface infection.

conditions.name: lagophthalmos
conditions.description: Incomplete eyelid closure that can leave the conjunctiva or cornea exposed.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The lids do not close fully; exposure may involve the conjunctiva alone or extend to the cornea.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine the extent of ocular exposure and the associated risk of corneal damage.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Classify closure according to whether the conjunctiva or cornea remains visible.

definitions.description: Some conjunctiva remains exposed, but the cornea is covered.
Any portion of the cornea remains exposed, however small.

follow_up.schedule: Assess eyelid closure and ocular appearance with a bright light at least once per shift throughout the ICU stay.
recommended_tests: Bright-light inspection of the eye and corneal clarity

conditions.name: corneal abrasion
conditions.description: A superficial injury that removes corneal epithelium and is the usual form of accidental corneal injury described in ICU.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The eye becomes red. An epithelial defect appears bright yellow after fluorescein dye is applied and viewed with blue light.

diagnostic_workup.test: Fluorescein dye eye drops and blue light
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Make the corneal epithelial defect visible.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The injury may be visible, although it is less apparent than with fluorescein dye and blue light.

follow_up.schedule: For an abrasion that has not improved in 24hrs, the patient-care summary calls for medical staff to be alerted.

conditions.name: Exposure keratopathy
conditions.description: Corneal surface drying associated with incomplete eyelid closure, increased tear evaporation and inadequate distribution of tears across the eye.
conditions.epidemiology: The document reports that it affects 20-42% of ICU patients. It also reports corneal epithelial defects attributable to this process in 60% of patients sedated for >48hours, including 42% within the first week.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The eye is red, and fluorescein dye can reveal epithelial defects of varying size that may resemble corneal abrasions. Persistent defects can produce scarring or, in severe cases, corneal perforation; secondary microbial keratitis can develop.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Staining reveals defects that can be indistinguishable in appearance from abrasions.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During ocular care and before another lubricant application.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Loss of corneal clarity warrants alerting medical staff.

follow_up.schedule: Inspect ocular appearance at least once per shift; examine the eye with a bright light before the next lubricant application in the every 4 hours care sequence.
long_term_effects: Corneal scarring after prolonged epithelial defects

conditions.name: Chemosis
conditions.description: Conjunctival oedema that makes the conjunctiva protrude. Impaired lid closure can contribute to chemosis, and chemosis can itself interfere with closure.
conditions.epidemiology: Described as common among ICU patients.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The conjunctiva is swollen and bulges outward; with severe oedema, it may protrude between closed eyelids.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognise conjunctival swelling and assess the ocular surface.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During regular ocular checks throughout the ICU stay.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Visible conjunctival swelling should prompt medical staff to be alerted and ophthalmological referral to be considered.

follow_up.schedule: Check ocular appearance at least once per shift throughout the ICU stay.
recommended_tests: Inspection of conjunctival swelling and eyelid closure

conditions.name: Conjunctivitis
conditions.description: In this ICU setting, conjunctivitis is usually bacterial and may be highly infectious and virulent.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A sticky eye is typical; redness is usual but is not always present in ICU. Marked redness without stickiness may have another cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a causative organism, including an unusual organism, and assess antibiotic sensitivity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When managing suspected conjunctivitis in ICU.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Sensitivity results can inform a change in treatment if the eye remains sticky or red.

diagnostic_workup.test: Inspection of ocular redness, discharge and corneal appearance
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for conjunctivitis and identify features needing ophthalmological assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an eye is sticky or red.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A dull cornea or new white patch calls for urgent ophthalmological assessment; a very red eye without stickiness may not be conjunctivitis.

follow_up.schedule: The main text calls for informing medical staff and seeking ophthalmic help if discharge and redness have not markedly improved in 48 hours. The patient-care summary instead says to alert medical staff if a red, sticky eye is no better in 24 HOURS.
recommended_tests: Inspection for corneal dullness or a white patch

conditions.name: Microbial keratitis
conditions.description: Infection of the cornea, to which a damaged corneal surface is particularly vulnerable. Deeper infection may cause severe, permanent ocular damage and loss of vision.
conditions.epidemiology: The document states that most cases are bacterial.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The eye is red and may be watery or sticky. A corneal ulcer has a fluorescein-staining epithelial defect over an underlying white/grey/yellowish opacity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect the epithelial defect over a corneal opacity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a corneal ulcer or microbial keratitis is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The epithelial defect stains with fluorescein dye.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an ophthalmologist finds keratitis in an ICU patient.
When the eye is red or a corneal abnormality is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An opacity that does not move when gently rinsed with saline raises concern for sight-threatening infection; adherent mucus moves.

long_term_effects: Permanent severe ocular damage and loss of vision from deeper infection

conditions.name: herpes simplex keratitis
conditions.description: A less common form of keratitis that may develop in debilitated patients.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Corneal epithelial dendrites and/or ulcers may stain yellow with fluorescein dye. The cornea may instead show grey areas that do not stain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess dendrites, ulcers and corneal staining.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When herpes simplex keratitis is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Dendrites or ulcers can stain yellow, although grey corneal areas may show no staining.

conditions.name: endogenous endophthalmitis
conditions.description: A sight-threatening infection inside the eye arising from the bloodstream during systemic infection; its presence also signals active systemic sepsis.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The eye may be red, sometimes less markedly than expected. A visible white line in front of the iris represents a level of pus in the anterior chamber, termed hypopyon.

subtypes.name: Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document describes it as particularly likely when hypopyon is present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognise possible endophthalmitis in a patient with sepsis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a septic patient has a red eye or a visible white line in front of the iris.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A white line representing pus in the anterior chamber warrants suspicion of endophthalmitis and immediate ophthalmic help.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Guide ophthalmic management when the systemic source is known.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis is suspected.

conditions.name: intraocular infection
conditions.description: Intraocular disease may accompany systemic fungal infection. The document notes that some systemic antifungal agents do not penetrate the eye sufficiently to treat it.
conditions.epidemiology: The document describes ocular involvement and intraocular disease that requires or is amenable to treatment, or requires additional intraocular treatment or vitrectomy, as having very low prevalence among patients with positive fungal cultures.
conditions.clinical_presentation: An ICU patient may be unable to report visual symptoms. A markedly abnormal eye, such as one with hypopyon or a cloudy pupil, requires examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible ocular involvement in systemic fungal infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Decide case by case for a patient with a positive fungal culture: an awake, asymptomatic patient does not need examination; an awake, symptomatic patient or one unable to report symptoms may need it; a patient with a very abnormal-appearing eye must be examined.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Decision-making and examination timing also take account of risk, prognosis, microbiology results, ocular penetration of current or planned treatment, patient position and feasibility of examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform the individual decision about ocular examination.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When systemic fungal infection is identified by culture.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive culture alone does not indicate routine ocular screening.

follow_up.schedule: Decisions about whether and when to examine the eye are made individually rather than through routine screening of every culture-positive patient.

conditions.name: ischaemic optic neuropathy
conditions.description: An ocular cause of blindness described after severe or recurrent hypotension, or reduced ocular perfusion associated with prone ventilation, raised ocular or orbital pressure and periocular swelling.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual loss or blindness may occur.

conditions.name: central retinal artery occlusion
conditions.description: A complication described in prone-ventilated patients when increased intraocular or intraorbital pressure, particularly alongside systemic hypotension, reduces ocular perfusion.

conditions.name: bilateral acute glaucoma
conditions.description: A rare complication in patients nursed prone, characterised by an abrupt increase in intraocular pressure and a risk of rapid visual loss from retinal or optic nerve ischaemia.
conditions.epidemiology: Described as rare among patients nursed prone.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The cornea becomes cloudy and grey, while the pupil is fixed in a mid-dilated position and does not respond to light.

diagnostic_workup.test: Examination of the cornea and pupillary light response
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognise findings requiring immediate ophthalmic treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When acute glaucoma is suspected in a prone patient.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cloudy grey cornea together with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil unresponsive to light is characteristic in the document.

conditions.name: acute primary angle closure glaucoma
conditions.description: Listed among potential ocular complications of direct eye pressure or increased orbital or ophthalmic pressure in prone patients.

conditions.name: orbital apex syndrome
conditions.description: An uncommon complication listed in prone patients exposed to direct ocular pressure or raised orbital or ophthalmic pressure.
conditions.epidemiology: Described as rare in this context.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual loss due to optic neuropathy occurs together with ophthalmoplegia involving multiple cranial nerves.

conditions.name: cortical blindness
conditions.description: A potential cause of visual loss in patients with profound hypotension lasting for an extended period.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with Grade 0 exposure: eyelids close completely.
decision_rules: Grade 0 exposure requires no protective intervention.
Continue checking eyelid closure and eye appearance with a bright light at least once per shift throughout the ICU stay.

response_assessment.timepoint: At least once per shift throughout the ICU stay
response_assessment.method: Examine eyelid closure and eye appearance with a bright light.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess the protective approach if exposure or an ocular abnormality develops.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with Grade 1 exposure: conjunctiva is visible, but the cornea is covered.
decision_rules: Provide ocular lubrication for Grade 1 exposure.
Alert medical staff if the cornea is not clear or the eye becomes red, sticky or swollen.

recommended_regimens.name: simple eye ointment
recommended_regimens.summary: Apply lubricant ointment into the space between the lower eyelid and conjunctiva, rather than over closed lids. Remove residual ointment with warm water before reapplication.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: four times daily; the supine-patient instructions specify every 4 hours

alternative_regimens.name: Lacrilube
alternative_regimens.summary: Named example of a lubricant ointment for ocular protection.

alternative_regimens.name: Xailin Night
alternative_regimens.summary: Named example of a lubricant ointment for ocular protection.

alternative_regimens.summary: Named example of a lubricant ointment for ocular protection.

response_assessment.timepoint: At least once per shift and before each new ointment application
response_assessment.method: Inspect eyelid closure and corneal clarity with a bright light.
response_assessment.interpretation: If corneal clarity is reduced, alert medical staff.

supportive_care: If the eye becomes red, sticky, swollen or shows a corneal abnormality, alert medical staff, consider ophthalmological referral and increase lubrication to every 2 hours.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Lubricant drops have a shorter duration of effect than ointment. Applying ointment over closed eyelids does not provide the intended ocular lubrication.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Conscious ICU patients who need ocular lubrication.
decision_rules: A conscious patient may receive lubricant drops at regular intervals, with ointment before sleep, instead of the ointment schedule used for other patients.

recommended_regimens.name: Hylotears
recommended_regimens.summary: Use lubricant drops while awake and supplement them with ointment before sleep.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Drops every 2 hours; ointment before sleep

response_assessment.timepoint: At least once per shift throughout the ICU stay
response_assessment.method: Inspect eyelid closure and eye appearance with a bright light.
response_assessment.interpretation: Alert medical staff if redness, discharge, swelling or a corneal abnormality appears.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Lid taping is not always needed and can distress conscious patients; repeated removal may injure or irritate eyelid or facial skin.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with Grade 2 exposure: any portion of the cornea remains uncovered.
decision_rules: Grade 2 exposure requires both lubrication and eyelid closure by taping or another suitable method.
Before securing the lids, ensure they are fully closed and that eyelashes do not touch the cornea.

recommended_regimens.name: simple eye ointment
recommended_regimens.summary: Clean away old ointment with warm water, inspect the eye, place fresh lubricant between the lower lid and conjunctiva, and then close the lids. Keep the outer lid surfaces free of ointment before applying tape.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: four times daily; the supine-patient instructions specify every 4 hours

recommended_regimens.name: Micropore tape
recommended_regimens.summary: After lubrication and complete lid closure, apply tape horizontally across the lids without allowing the tape or eyelashes to contact the cornea.

alternative_regimens.name: cling film
alternative_regimens.summary: Cover each eye with a 10x10cm square as an alternative to tape; replace it each shift.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When an alternative method of protecting the closed eye is appropriate.

alternative_regimens.name: Kerrapro
alternative_regimens.summary: A hydrogel or silicone dressing or pad may replace taping; change it once per shift and prevent drying or poor positioning.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When oedema prevents manual eyelid closure; use with great care to avoid eye injury.

alternative_regimens.name: Gelliperm
alternative_regimens.summary: A hydrogel or silicone dressing or pad may replace taping; change it once per shift and prevent drying or poor positioning.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When oedema prevents manual eyelid closure; use with great care to avoid eye injury.

not_recommended.name: Unnecessary lid taping
not_recommended.reason: It may distress patients or relatives, and repeated tape removal can damage or irritate the skin or eyelids.

response_assessment.timepoint: At least once per shift and before each new lubricant application
response_assessment.method: Check eye appearance and corneal clarity using a bright light.
response_assessment.interpretation: Alert medical staff if the cornea is not clear or another ocular abnormality is present.

supportive_care: Do not use the same cling film roll for different patients.
If redness, stickiness, chemosis or a corneal abnormality develops, alert medical staff, consider ophthalmological referral and increase lubrication to every 2 hours.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Incorrectly placed tape or eyelashes rubbing against the cornea can cause more injury than the protective measure prevents.

decision_rules: Treat prone positioning in an unconscious patient as a major ocular risk regardless of the observed exposure grade.
Lubricate the eyes and secure the eyelids closed.
Contact medical staff if severe oedema allows swollen conjunctiva to protrude through the closed eyelids; temporary closure with sutures may be necessary.

recommended_regimens.name: simple eye ointment
recommended_regimens.summary: Clean and inspect the eyes, apply lubricant to the ocular surface, and close the lids while keeping eyelashes away from the cornea.

recommended_regimens.name: Micropore tape
recommended_regimens.summary: Secure fully closed lids horizontally after applying ointment, ensuring that the lashes remain outside the eye.

alternative_regimens.name: cling film
alternative_regimens.summary: Use over the closed, lubricated eyes instead of tape.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Alternative protection for an unconscious prone patient.

response_assessment.timepoint: At least once per shift and before re-lubrication
response_assessment.method: Check corneal clarity with a bright light and examine eyelid closure.
response_assessment.interpretation: Alert medical staff if the cornea is not clear.

supportive_care: Prevent direct compression of the eyes with a 3-pin head holder, gel rings or a similar device.
Relieve pressure on the eyes where possible.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Prone patients may develop facial, eyelid or conjunctival oedema. Direct pressure or raised orbital or ocular pressure may impair ocular perfusion and cause permanent visual loss.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with a simple corneal abrasion and no secondary infection.
decision_rules: A superficial epithelial defect can be assessed with fluorescein dye and blue light; it is less conspicuous under white light.
Increase lubrication and tape the lids if there is significant unwanted corneal exposure.
Alert medical staff if an abrasion has not improved in 24hrs in the red-eye instructions, or if a corneal opacity develops.

recommended_regimens.name: chloramphenicol ointment
recommended_regimens.summary: May be used for an uncomplicated abrasion without secondary infection, alongside increased ocular lubrication and exposure control when needed.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: four times daily for 5 to 7 days

response_assessment.method: Reassess an abrasion in a red eye for improvement and inspect the cornea for opacity.
response_assessment.interpretation: If the abrasion has not improved, an opacity is present or the cause remains uncertain, alert medical staff.

supportive_care: Check the lubrication schedule and consider lid taping when exposure contributes to the abrasion.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: An epithelial defect caused by exposure keratopathy may resemble a traumatic abrasion. A dull cornea or white patch requires urgent ophthalmological assessment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with a sticky eye, usually accompanied by redness.
decision_rules: Consider a swab of ocular discharge for microbial culture because unusual organisms are more likely in this setting.
A markedly red eye without stickiness may have another cause and requires expert ophthalmological help.
If culture suggests chloramphenicol resistance but the eye is improving, do not change treatment.

If the eye remains sticky or red and the organism is not sensitive to chloramphenicol, treatment may be changed to an ointment containing an antibiotic to which the organism is sensitive, or other antibiotic drops may be used with simple lubricant ointment.
Seek urgent ophthalmological assessment if the cornea becomes dull or develops a white patch.

recommended_regimens.name: chloramphenicol ointment
recommended_regimens.summary: Apply into the eye for suspected conjunctivitis; ointment is preferred to drops here because it also provides sustained lubrication.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: four times a day for 5-7 days

alternative_regimens.name: Antibiotic ointment selected by microbial sensitivity
alternative_regimens.summary: An ointment containing an antibiotic active against the cultured organism may replace chloramphenicol ointment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The organism is not sensitive to chloramphenicol and the eye remains sticky or red.

alternative_regimens.name: Other antibiotic drops with simple lubricant ointment
alternative_regimens.summary: Use active antibiotic drops together with lubricant ointment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The organism is not sensitive to chloramphenicol and the eye remains sticky or red.

not_recommended.name: Changing chloramphenicol ointment solely because of a nonsensitive culture result when the eye is improving
not_recommended.reason: The guidance says to leave treatment unchanged if the eye is getting better.

response_assessment.method: Assess whether ocular discharge and redness have improved markedly.
response_assessment.interpretation: If they have not, inform medical staff and seek ophthalmic help.

response_assessment.method: Assess the red, sticky eye for improvement under the summary instructions.
response_assessment.interpretation: If it is no better, alert medical staff. This threshold differs from the 48 hours threshold in the conjunctivitis management text.

supportive_care: Remove discharge by bathing the eyelids with warm water, using different gauze for each eye.
Take precautions against transmission to other patients and staff.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In ICU, conjunctivitis is usually bacterial and may be highly infectious.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with suspected corneal infection, including a red eye with a corneal ulcer, opacity or other concerning corneal lesion.
decision_rules: Seek urgent ophthalmic help for a suspicious corneal lesion.
For ophthalmologists managing keratitis, obtain a corneal scrape and begin appropriate intensive topical antibiotic treatment immediately.
Try to avoid lid taping because it may promote bacterial growth; continue generous ointment lubrication.

recommended_regimens.name: fluoroquinolone
recommended_regimens.summary: Start appropriate intensive topical antibiotic therapy immediately after arranging a corneal scrape for keratitis.

not_recommended.name: Lid taping during keratitis when avoidable

response_assessment.timepoint: Immediately when a corneal abnormality is seen
response_assessment.method: Inspect for a corneal opacity and, where appropriate, use fluorescein to identify an overlying epithelial defect or dendritic lesion.
response_assessment.interpretation: A concerning corneal lesion warrants urgent ophthalmic assessment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guidance identifies virulent bacteria, particularly Pseudomonas, as likely causes in this setting. It also describes herpes simplex keratitis as a less common possibility in debilitated patients; suspected cases require urgent ophthalmic help.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Septic ICU patients with suspected intraocular infection, particularly those with a hypopyon.
decision_rules: Obtain immediate ophthalmic help when endogenous endophthalmitis is suspected.
For suspected bacterial disease, use the known systemic infection to guide management. If it is unknown, urgently sample and inject using the stated antibiotic protocol.
If the platelet count is <30,000, request platelets before the procedure because of vitreous haemorrhage risk.

recommended_regimens.name: amikacin and vancomycin
recommended_regimens.summary: Use the urgent ocular tap-and-inject protocol for suspected endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis when the systemic infection does not identify the organism.

response_assessment.method: Look for a white line of pus in front of the iris, even when ocular redness is less marked than expected.
response_assessment.interpretation: A hypopyon raises suspicion of sight-threatening endophthalmitis and indicates active systemic sepsis.

supportive_care: Request platelet administration before ocular sampling and injection if the platelet count is <30,000.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: This is a sight-threatening emergency associated with bloodstream spread of infection.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with cystic fibrosis and endophthalmitis.
decision_rules: In a patient with cystic fibrosis, consider aspergillus first as the cause of endophthalmitis.
Do not stop voriconazole solely because a reversible visual aura occurs.

recommended_regimens.name: voriconazole
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as first-line treatment for endophthalmitis in a patient with cystic fibrosis, while considering aspergillus first as the possible cause.

not_recommended.name: Stopping voriconazole solely for visual aura
not_recommended.reason: The guidance describes these auras as fully reversible after the drug is stopped and says they are not an indication to stop it.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guidance states that patients with cystic fibrosis are usually colonised with aspergillus.

treatment_pathways.condition: Systemic fungal infection and the eye
treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients with a positive fungal culture, including those who cannot report visual symptoms.
decision_rules: Decide whether and when to perform an ophthalmological examination individually rather than screening every culture-positive patient.
An awake patient without symptoms does not require examination under the stated criteria.
An awake patient with symptoms, or a patient unable to report symptoms, may need examination.
Examine a patient whose eye looks very abnormal, such as with hypopyon, a cloudy pupil or possible ocular perforation.
Base the individual decision and its timing on risk, prognosis, microbiology, ocular penetration of current or planned treatment, patient position and whether examination is feasible.
If intraocular infection is present, coordinate with microbiologists and ophthalmologists to select an antifungal with good ocular penetration.

not_recommended.name: Routine ophthalmological screening of all patients with positive fungal cultures
not_recommended.reason: The guidance says that eye involvement and intraocular disease requiring or amenable to treatment, additional intraocular treatment or vitrectomy are very uncommon, so routine screening is not indicated.

response_assessment.method: Review symptoms, eye appearance, individual risk and the feasibility of examination.
response_assessment.interpretation: A very abnormal eye requires examination; symptoms or inability to report them may warrant examination.

supportive_care: For confirmed intraocular infection, liaise with microbiologists and ophthalmologists about antifungal ocular penetration.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Not all systemic antifungal agents reach the eye sufficiently to treat intraocular disease, and ICU patients may be unable to describe visual symptoms.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients nursed prone who develop findings suggestive of an acute rise in intraocular pressure.
decision_rules: Arrange immediate ophthalmic treatment if the cornea becomes cloudy and grey and the pupil is fixed in a mid-dilated position without a light response.

response_assessment.method: Inspect corneal appearance and pupil position and light response.
response_assessment.interpretation: The described findings require immediate ophthalmic treatment because visual loss can occur quickly.

supportive_care: Relieve direct pressure on the eyes where possible in prone patients.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guidance specifies urgency but does not name a treatment regimen for this condition.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: ICU patients prescribed multiple ocular drops or both drops and ointment.
decision_rules: Separate different eye drops to avoid one washing away another.
Administer drops before ointment because ointment impedes entry of drops into ocular tissues.
If lid closure is poor, manually close the lids after instilling ointment to spread it over the ocular surface.

not_recommended.name: Simultaneous administration of different eye drops
not_recommended.reason: One medication may wash away another and reduce its effect.

not_recommended.name: Applying ointment before prescribed drops
not_recommended.reason: The ointment repels water and can prevent the drops from entering ocular tissues.

supportive_care: Leave ideally 5 minutes and at least 1 minute between different eye medications.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: These administration instructions apply when ocular treatment has already been prescribed.

special_populations.considerations: The need for eye protection depends on eyelid closure. Grade 0 indicates complete closure; Grade 1 indicates conjunctival exposure without corneal exposure; Grade 2 indicates any corneal exposure and carries a major risk of corneal injury.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Grade 0 requires no protective intervention. For Grade 1, lubricate the eyes every 4 hours. For Grade 2, lubricate every 4 hours and close the lids with tape or cling film. Check corneal clarity with a bright light and alert medical staff if the cornea is not clear.

special_populations.considerations: All are at major risk of eye injury. Facial and eyelid oedema and chemosis are common; direct compression or increased pressure around the eye can impair ocular perfusion and cause permanent visual loss.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Reapply eye lubricant every 4 hours and close the lids with tape or cling film. Check corneal clarity with a bright light and alert medical staff if it is not clear. Prevent direct pressure on the eyes where possible. Contact medical staff if severe swelling causes the conjunctiva to protrude between closed lids, as temporary suturing may be needed.

special_populations.considerations: Repeated lid taping can distress conscious patients and may injure or irritate the eyelids or facial skin.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: An alternative to lubricant ointment four times daily is lubricant drops every 2 hours, with ointment before sleep. Tape the lids only when necessary.

special_populations.considerations: Intraocular involvement is possible, and patients in ICU may be unable to report visual symptoms. Routine eye screening of every culture-positive patient is not indicated; decisions about examination and its timing depend on individual risk, symptoms, eye appearance and other clinical factors.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: An awake, asymptomatic patient does not require examination. An awake patient with symptoms, or one unable to report symptoms, may need examination. A markedly abnormal eye, such as one with hypopyon, a cloudy pupil or possible ocular perforation, must be examined. If intraocular infection is present, coordinate with microbiologists and ophthalmologists to use an antifungal with adequate ocular penetration.

special_populations.considerations: When endophthalmitis occurs, the guidance advises considering aspergillus first because these patients are usually colonised with it.

special_populations.population: Patients with low platelet count undergoing a procedure for endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis
special_populations.considerations: A platelet count of <30,000 increases the risk of vitreous haemorrhage during the procedure.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Request platelets before performing the procedure.

special_populations.population: Patients with profound or recurrent hypotension
special_populations.considerations: Severe or recurrent hypotension can cause visual loss from ischaemic optic neuropathy. Profound hypotension sustained for extended periods may also cause cortical blindness.

recommendations.statement: Assess eyelid closure and inspect the eyes with a bright light at least once per shift throughout the ICU stay.
recommendations.context: Routine eye protection and surveillance.

recommendations.statement: If an eye is red, sticky or chemosed, or the cornea appears abnormal, notify medical staff, consider an ophthalmological opinion and increase lubrication to every 2 hours.
recommendations.context: Abnormal findings during routine eye assessment.

recommendations.statement: Assess the severity of incomplete eyelid closure using the document's exposure grades.
recommendations.context: Grade 0 indicates fully closed lids; Grade 1 indicates exposed conjunctiva without exposed cornea; Grade 2 indicates any corneal exposure.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of lid closure and risk of corneal damage

recommendations.statement: Take no protective action for Grade 0 exposure, provide lubrication for Grade 1 exposure, and provide both lubrication and eyelid taping or another means of lid closure for Grade 2 exposure.
recommendations.context: Actions are determined by the degree of eye exposure, not by a recommendation grade.

recommendations.statement: Apply a generous amount of lubricant ointment into the eye four times daily, rather than over closed eyelids; options given are simple eye ointment, Lacrilube, Xailin Night and VitA-POS.
recommendations.context: Ocular surface protection.
recommendations.rationale: Drops have a shorter duration of effect, and ointment applied into the eye protects better than manual eyelid closure alone.

recommendations.statement: For a conscious patient, 2 hourly lubricant drops, such as Hylotears, together with ointment before sleep are an alternative.
recommendations.context: Ocular surface protection in conscious patients.

recommendations.statement: Tape eyelids closed only when necessary. When taping is used, close the lids fully and keep the tape away from the eye surface.
recommendations.context: Eyelid closure when exposure requires protection.
recommendations.rationale: Taping can distress patients or relatives, repeated removal can injure or irritate skin or lids, and incorrectly positioned tape can damage the eye.

recommendations.statement: Cling film may replace tape: place a 10x10cm square over each eye, replace it every shift and never use the same roll for different patients.
recommendations.context: Alternative eye covering.
recommendations.rationale: Unlike tape, cling film does not damage the eye if it touches the eyeball.

recommendations.statement: If oedema prevents manual eyelid closure, hydrogel or silicone dressings or pads, such as Kerrapro or Gelliperm, may replace tape. Change them once per shift and take great care that they remain moist and correctly positioned.
recommendations.context: Eyelid protection in the presence of oedema.
recommendations.rationale: A dressing that dries or shifts can injure the eye.

recommendations.statement: Every 4 hours, first wash away dried ointment with warm water, then inspect the eye for abnormalities using a bright light before applying fresh ointment to the eye surface between the lower lid and conjunctiva.
recommendations.context: Routine lubricant application.

recommendations.statement: When taping follows ointment application, close the lids, check that the lashes are clear of the cornea, remove ointment from the outside of the eye and apply Micropore tape horizontally across the lids.
recommendations.context: Sequence for lubrication and eyelid taping.
recommendations.rationale: Lashes against the cornea can cause an iatrogenic abrasion, while ointment on the outside of the eye interferes with tape adhesion.

recommendations.statement: For an unconscious patient nursed prone, reapply eye lubricant every 4 hours and keep the eyelids closed with tape or cling film.
recommendations.context: Prone, unconscious patients.
recommendations.rationale: Facial and eyelid oedema, chemosis and corneal exposure can occur in this setting.

recommendations.statement: Avoid direct pressure on the eyes of prone patients by using a 3-pin head holder, gel rings or a similar device.
recommendations.context: Prone positioning.
recommendations.rationale: Prone positioning can compress the eyes directly.

recommendations.statement: Contact medical staff if severe oedema causes swollen conjunctiva to protrude through closed eyelids; temporary eyelid closure with sutures may be needed.
recommendations.context: Severe chemosis during prone care.

recommendations.statement: A simple corneal abrasion without secondary infection can be treated with chloramphenicol ointment four times daily for 5 to 7 days. Increase lubrication and tape the lids if unwanted corneal exposure is substantial.
recommendations.context: Treatment of an uncomplicated abrasion.

recommendations.statement: Perform endotracheal suctioning from the patient's side rather than above the head, with the eyes covered.
recommendations.context: Prevention of ocular surface infection during suctioning.
recommendations.rationale: Respiratory secretions are thought to be a major source of ocular infection, and these measures can reduce Pseudomonas infection rates.

recommendations.statement: Look for a sticky eye when assessing for conjunctivitis, while recognizing that redness is not always present in ICU patients. Seek expert ophthalmological help for an eye that is very red but not sticky.
recommendations.context: Assessment of a red eye.
recommendations.rationale: Marked redness without discharge may have a cause other than conjunctivitis.

recommendations.statement: Consider swabbing eye discharge for microbial culture, and remove discharge by washing the eyelids with warm water and using separate gauze for each eye.
recommendations.context: Initial management of conjunctivitis.
recommendations.rationale: Unusual infecting organisms are more likely in this setting.

recommendations.statement: Apply chloramphenicol ointment into the eye four times a day for 5-7 days to treat conjunctivitis.
recommendations.context: Treatment of conjunctivitis in ICU.
recommendations.rationale: The ointment provides more sustained lubrication than drops.

recommendations.statement: If culture suggests the organism is not sensitive to chloramphenicol but the eye is improving, do not change treatment. If stickiness or redness persists, the ointment can be changed to one containing an antibiotic to which the organism is sensitive, or other antibiotic drops can be added alongside simple lubricant ointment.
recommendations.context: Adjustment of conjunctivitis treatment after microbial results.

recommendations.statement: Inform medical staff and seek ophthalmic help if discharge and redness have not improved markedly in 48 hours.
recommendations.context: Follow-up of conjunctivitis; a later summary table instead specifies alerting medical staff if a red, sticky eye is no better in 24 HOURS.

recommendations.statement: Seek an urgent ophthalmological opinion if the cornea becomes dull or develops a white patch.
recommendations.context: Possible corneal infection during assessment or treatment of conjunctivitis.

recommendations.statement: Seek urgent ophthalmic help when corneal findings suggest microbial keratitis or herpes simplex keratitis.
recommendations.context: Concerning findings include an ulcer over a white, grey or yellowish opacity, a corneal dendrite, or a non-staining grey corneal area.
recommendations.rationale: Deep corneal infection can cause severe permanent damage and vision loss.

recommendations.statement: Obtain immediate ophthalmic help if endogenous endophthalmitis is suspected in a septic patient, particularly when a white line of pus is visible in front of the iris.
recommendations.context: A hypopyon indicates possible infection inside the eye.
recommendations.rationale: This is a sight-threatening emergency and indicates active systemic sepsis.

Decide whether and when to examine each patient individually, considering risk, prognosis, microbiology results, the ocular penetration of current or planned treatment, patient position and feasibility of examination.
