document_sections.heading: 1 Summary
document_sections.content: This guidance is intended mainly for ICU staff without ophthalmic training. It addresses prevention of eye problems in vulnerable patients, recognition of ocular disease that may warrant ophthalmic referral, and administration of prescribed eye treatment. Its principal focus is the ocular surface, although it also addresses less common conditions.

document_sections.heading: 2 Introduction
document_sections.content: Tear production, blinking and eyelid closure help maintain the cornea and the front of the eye. In ICU, these functions may be impaired by facial oedema, reduced consciousness, neurological injury, airflow from CPAP or oxygen masks, muscle relaxants, sedation, or prolonged prone positioning. Patients who cannot close their eyes or blink substantially less often face greater risk of anterior eye damage. Risk is higher during mechanical ventilation because of longer stays, sedating or paralysing medicines, and positive-pressure ventilation. Potential problems include superficial corneal abrasion, exposure keratopathy, chemosis, microbial conjunctivitis and microbial keratitis. Eye-care protocols may be applied inconsistently, and records of care are often inadequate. A clear assessment and intervention protocol, followed correctly and consistently, can prevent most corneal problems.

document_sections.heading: 3 Protecting the eye
document_sections.content: Throughout an ICU stay, staff should inspect eyelid closure and the eye with a bright light at least once per shift. A red or sticky eye, chemosis, or a corneal abnormality calls for medical staff to be alerted, consideration of ophthalmic referral, and increased lubrication every 2 hours.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of lid closure and risk of corneal damage
document_sections.content: Lagophthalmos means incomplete eyelid closure, and its severity must be assessed when the eyes do not close properly. Grade 0 means complete closure; Grade 1 means visible conjunctiva without corneal exposure; Grade 2 means any corneal exposure, however small.

document_sections.heading: Protective measures
document_sections.content: Protection depends on exposure grade: Grade 0 needs no intervention, Grade 1 needs lubrication, and Grade 2 needs both lubrication and taping or another means of closing the lids.

document_sections.heading: The methods to protect the eyes are:
document_sections.content: Lubricating ointment should be placed generously inside the eye four times daily; examples are simple eye ointment, Lacrilube, Xailin Night and VitA-POS. Drops have a shorter duration of effect, and ointment placed on closed lids does not provide the intended application. Ointment applied into the eye is preferable to manual closure alone. For a conscious patient, lubricant drops such as Hylotears every 2 hours, followed by ointment before sleep, are an alternative. Eyelids can be closed manually or taped. Taping is not always needed; it can distress relatives or conscious patients, and repeated removal can injure or irritate facial or eyelid skin. It should be used only when necessary, with lids fully closed and tape kept off the ocular surface, since incorrect taping can cause more injury than it prevents. Cling film is an alternative that does not damage the eye if it touches the eyeball: use a 10x10cm square over each eye, replace it every shift, and never share a roll between patients. If oedema prevents manual lid closure, hydrogel or silicone dressings or pads, such as Kerrapro or Gelliperm, may replace tape. Replace them once per shift; drying or poor positioning can injure the eye, so their use requires great care.

document_sections.heading: What order to do this: Every 4 hours:
document_sections.content: First wash the eyes with warm water to remove old ointment, then inspect them for abnormalities with a bright light before applying more lubricant. Pull down the lower lid and place new ointment into the space between that lid and the conjunctiva. If taping is needed, apply ointment before closing the eyes. Check that eyelashes do not touch the cornea, remove ointment from the outside of the lids so tape will adhere, and seal the closed lids with horizontally placed Micropore tape.

document_sections.heading: Prone unconscious patients.
document_sections.content: Prone positioning in an unconscious patient can produce facial and eyelid oedema and commonly causes chemosis. As in other ventilated patients, exposure keratopathy may occur. Direct pressure on the eye can be avoided with a 3-pin head holder of the type used in prone spinal surgery, gel rings, or similar devices. Always reapply lubricant every 4 hours and close the lids with tape or cling film as described above. If severe oedema causes swollen conjunctiva to protrude between closed lids, contact medical staff; temporary suturing of the lids may be required.

document_sections.heading: 4 Identifying disease of the eye
document_sections.content: The following sections distinguish ocular surface injury, conjunctival swelling and infection from other causes of an abnormal eye in ICU.

document_sections.heading: Exposure keratopathy and corneal abrasion
document_sections.content: Accidental corneal injury in ICU is almost always a superficial abrasion that removes surface epithelium and makes the eye red. Fluorescein drops viewed with blue light make the epithelial defect appear bright yellow; white light can also show it, less clearly. Exposure keratopathy is corneal dryness caused by incomplete lid closure, excessive tear evaporation and inadequate distribution of tears across the ocular surface. It causes redness and fluorescein-visible epithelial defects of varying size that may look like abrasions. It affects 20-42% of ICU patients; among patients sedated for >48hours, 60% develop corneal epithelial defects, including 42% within the first week. Persistent defects may scar and, in severe cases, perforate the cornea; microbial keratitis can develop secondarily. A simple abrasion without secondary infection can be treated with chloramphenicol ointment four times daily for 5 to 7 days, alongside more lubrication and lid taping when unwanted corneal exposure is substantial. The illustration compares an eye before fluorescein with a blue-light fluorescein view showing an abrasion.

document_sections.heading: Chemosis
document_sections.content: Chemosis is conjunctival oedema that makes the conjunctiva bulge and is common in ICU. Risk factors include impaired venous drainage from positive-pressure ventilation, rising positive end-expiratory pressure or tight endotracheal-tube tape; generalised oedema associated with fluid overload or hypalbuminaemia; increased hydrostatic pressure from prolonged recumbency or prone ventilation; and increased capillary leakage during systemic inflammatory responses. Chemosis may prevent proper eyelid closure, while incomplete closure may also promote chemosis.

document_sections.heading: Microbial infections
document_sections.content: Bacterial colonisation of the eye becomes more common over time in ICU. Among ventilated medical patients, as many as 77% carry at least one abnormal bacterial species after 7-42 days; 40% of patients receiving prolonged ventilation and sedation carry multiple bacterial species. The organisms most often isolated are Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Respiratory secretions are thought to be the main source of ocular surface infection; aerosols during tracheal suction and direct contact with suction catheters are implicated. Pseudomonas infection rates can be reduced by suctioning the endotracheal tube from the patient's side rather than above the head and by covering the eyes.

document_sections.heading: Conjunctivitis:
document_sections.content: Staff should look for stickiness; the eye is usually red, although redness may be absent in ICU. A very red eye without stickiness may have another cause and requires expert ophthalmic advice. Conjunctivitis in this setting is usually bacterial and may be highly infectious and virulent, with potential transmission to staff and other patients.

document_sections.heading: Management of conjunctivitis:
document_sections.content: Taking an eye-discharge swab for microbial culture is advisable because unusual organisms are more likely. Clean discharge from the lids with warm water, using different gauze for each eye. Put chloramphenicol ointment, rather than drops, inside the eye four times a day for 5-7 days to retain the ointment's lubricating benefit. If culture indicates resistance to chloramphenicol but the eye has improved, do not change treatment. If redness or stickiness persists, the ointment may be changed to one containing an antibiotic to which the organism is sensitive; alternatively, other antibiotic drops may be added to simple lubricant ointment. Inform medical staff and seek ophthalmic help if discharge and redness have not improved markedly within 48 hours. A dull cornea or a new white patch requires urgent ophthalmic assessment.

document_sections.heading: Microbial keratitis:
document_sections.content: A damaged cornea, including one affected by exposure keratopathy, is particularly susceptible to rapidly developing bacterial invasion. Infection may remain superficial, but deeper infection can cause severe permanent injury and loss of vision. Most cases are bacterial and present with a red, possibly watery or sticky eye and a corneal ulcer: a fluorescein-staining epithelial defect over a white, grey or yellowish opacity. Less often, debilitated patients develop herpes simplex keratitis, which may show epithelial dendrites or ulcers staining yellow with fluorescein, or non-staining grey corneal areas. Any of these findings requires urgent ophthalmic help.

document_sections.heading: 5 Rare eye conditions in ICU
document_sections.content: In addition to ocular surface disease, ICU patients may develop uncommon conditions that threaten sight.

document_sections.heading: Red eye in a septic patient: possible endogenous endophthalmitis
document_sections.content: Endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious infection inside the eye arising from bloodstream spread of systemic infection. The eye may be red, sometimes less than expected. A visible white line in front of the iris is a hypopyon, a level of pus within the eye, and should raise suspicion of endophthalmitis. Seek immediate ophthalmic help: this is a sight-threatening emergency and a sign of active systemic sepsis.

document_sections.heading: Other problems
document_sections.content: Severe or repeated hypotension can cause blindness through ischaemic optic neuropathy. In prone ventilated patients, raised intraocular or intraorbital pressure with pronounced periocular swelling may reduce ocular perfusion, particularly when systemic hypotension is also present. This can lead to ischaemic optic neuropathy, central retinal artery occlusion and permanent visual loss. Rarely, prone patients develop bilateral acute glaucoma, with a sudden increase in intraocular pressure that can rapidly impair vision through retinal or optic-nerve ischaemia. A cloudy grey cornea and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil unresponsive to light indicate this condition, which needs immediate ophthalmic treatment.

document_sections.heading: 6 Delivering treatment to the eye when it is prescribed
document_sections.content: Eye medicines are generally drops or ointment, and several different drops may be prescribed. Do not administer different drops together because one can wash away another and reduce its effect. Separate medicines by ideally 5 minutes and at least 1 minute. Give drops before ointment, since ointment repels water and obstructs drop penetration. Where lid closure is poor, manually close the lids after inserting ointment to distribute it across the entire ocular surface.

document_sections.heading: 7. Systemic fungal infection and the eye
document_sections.content: Any systemic fungal infection may involve the eye. ICU patients may be unable to report visual symptoms, and some systemic antifungals do not enter the eye sufficiently to treat intraocular infection. Earlier guidelines often advised urgent ophthalmic assessment for every patient with a blood or line-tip culture positive for candida, aspergillus or another fungus. More recent evidence indicates that ocular involvement and intraocular disease requiring, responding to, or needing additional intraocular treatment or vitrectomy are very uncommon; routine screening of every culture-positive patient is therefore not indicated. The guidance recommends deciding on screening exceptionally, case by case, according to individual risk, symptoms and ocular appearance. An awake, asymptomatic patient needs no examination; an awake patient with symptoms or a patient unable to report symptoms may need one. A markedly abnormal eye, such as one with hypopyon, a cloudy pupil or possible ocular perforation, must be examined. The decision and timing should also consider risk, prognosis, microbiology, penetration of current or planned treatment into the eye, patient position and whether examination is feasible. If intraocular infection is present, work with microbiologists and ophthalmologists to select an appropriate antifungal with good ocular penetration.

document_sections.heading: 8. Tips for ophthalmologists seeing patients in ICU
document_sections.content: If exposure requires taping, check that the eyelashes cannot rub the cornea. Keratitis is most likely to involve virulent bacteria, particularly pseudomonas: perform a corneal scrape and immediately begin appropriate intensive topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic treatment. Try not to tape the lids, as this may encourage bacterial growth; instead, use ample ointment for lubrication. G tropicamide 1% and G. phenylephrine 2.5% may safely be used for dilation. Record clearly that dilation was performed, when the drops were given and how long the pupils are expected not to react to light, about 4 hours. Suspect endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis especially when hypopyon is present. Use a known systemic infection to guide treatment; otherwise, urgently perform a tap and inject according to the amikacin and vancomycin protocol. With a platelet count <30,000, vitreous haemorrhage is a risk, so request platelets before the procedure. In a patient with cystic fibrosis and endophthalmitis, consider aspergillus first because these patients are usually colonised with it; use voriconazole as first-line treatment. Patients taking voriconazole may experience visual aura because it inhibits cytochrome P450, which is present in retinal pigment epithelium. The aura resolve completely after stopping the medicine and are not themselves a reason to stop it. Prone positioning may directly compress the eyes or raise orbital or ophthalmic pressure through gravity or periocular swelling. Possible consequences are acute primary angle closure glaucoma, ischaemic optic neuropathy, vascular occlusion and, rarely, orbital apex syndrome, in which optic neuropathy causes visual loss alongside ophthalmoplegia affecting multiple cranial nerves. Relieve pressure on the eyes where possible. Prolonged profound hypotension may cause visual loss through ischaemic optic neuropathy or cortical blindness.

document_sections.heading: Patient nursed supine and unconscious
document_sections.content: The table assigns eye-protection actions by lid-closure grade. Grade 0, with good closure, needs no action. For Grade 1 conjunctival exposure, lubricate every 4 hours, inspect corneal clarity with a bright light, alert medical staff if it is not clear, remove old ointment, and place fresh ointment between the lower lid and conjunctiva. Grade 2, with conjunctival and some corneal exposure, is identified as a major risk: provide lubrication and lid taping or cling film. Check corneal clarity and alert medical staff if it is reduced. Apply ointment as for Grade 1, close the lids with eyelashes outside the eye and no ointment on the lids, then use horizontal micropore tape or 10x10cm clingfilm.

document_sections.heading: Patient nursed prone and unconscious: Major risk to eye in all cases
document_sections.content: All unconscious prone patients are described as having major eye risk and needing lubrication and taped lids. Inspect corneal clarity with a bright light and alert medical staff if the cornea is not clear. Apply ointment as for Grade 2, close the lids with lashes outside the eye and ointment removed from the lids, and place micropore tape horizontally. The subsequent comparison table distinguishes a red sticky eye from a red eye without stickiness. For a sticky eye, take a swab and use chloramphenicol ointment X 4/DAY; the condition can spread to other patients. The table says to alert medical staff if there is no improvement in 24 HOURS. For a red eye without stickiness, assess whether the cornea is clear or stains with fluorescein. With a clear cornea or simple abrasion, review lubrication and consider lid taping. Alert medical staff if there is corneal opacity, an abrasion has not improved in 24hrs, or the cause is uncertain. The table's 24-hour instruction for a sticky eye differs from the 48 hours stated in the conjunctivitis management text.

document_sections.heading: Eye opacities on or inside eye: ALERT MEDICAL STAFF IMMEDIATELY
document_sections.content: An opacity on or inside the eye calls for immediate notification of medical staff. Gently rinsing with saline helps distinguish adherent mucus, which moves, from an opacity. Suspect sight-threatening infection and alert medical staff immediately if a corneal opacity remains in place after rinsing or a white line is visible at the bottom of the iris.
